saint_pick.name: Agapius
saint_pick.selection_reason: Agapius has the best-documented story of the group: Eusebius, a near-contemporary eyewitness in Caesarea, records in The Martyrs of Palestine how he was condemned to the beasts in AD 306, offered a pardon, refused it, was mauled by a bear and survived, and was later drowned with weights tied to his feet. Strictly, the bear episode is a survival rather than a formally examined miracle, so it is a borderline fit for the miracle-led brief. The other candidates have thinner or legendary sources: Maurus of Parentium is the only one with a Nov 21 commemoration, but his story is mostly legend.
saint_pick.catholic_veneration: Martyr venerated in the Roman Martyrology (Latin Church); listed by Santi e Beati and Nominis as a saint of the Catholic Church. I am not certain of his exact calendar date, so check it before posting.

claims.claim: Agapius was a Christian martyr at Caesarea in Palestine in the early fourth century, around 306.
His story is told by Eusebius of Caesarea, who wrote close to the events of the persecution.
He was tortured several times but always held back for greater trials.
Before Maximinus in the amphitheater, he was offered freedom if he would abandon the Christian faith, and he refused.
A bear was loosed against him and wounded him without killing him.
According to tradition, the next day stones were tied to his feet and he was drowned in the sea.
The reason the source attributes to him is faithfulness to the Creator.
He is listed in the Roman Martyrology on November 21.
The persecution began in the Roman Empire in 303 under the tetrarchy.
Caesarea Maritima was the seat of the provincial government and a major city of the eastern Mediterranean.
Eusebius, later bishop of Caesarea, gathered accounts of persecuted Christians; his work is a Christian record of memory, not a Roman administrative register.
Eusebius's account survives in a short Greek version and a longer version preserved mainly in Syriac, published by William Cureton in the nineteenth century.
The longer version gives more detail and words attributed to the condemned, which cannot be treated as a verified transcript.
Nothing certain is known of his birth, family or profession; nor is the place of burial or the fate of his body known.
The Greek text says he survived a day before the drowning; the sequence is attested by Eusebius, and the most dramatic details should be read within the language of ancient martyr literature.

Eusebius places the event in the fourth year of the persecution and links Maximinus's arrival to a day in November; tradition has read this as November 20, 306 for the arena and the next day for the death.
Older calendars also knew November 20; the present Catholic memorial is November 21.
Eusebius also tells of another Agapius, beheaded at Caesarea with seven companions; the two accounts must not be merged, and that group is commemorated in the East on March 15.
Some ancient calendars commemorated Agapius together with Timothy and Thecla, and he entered the Latin martyrologies relatively late.
The Roman Martyrology praises him as tortured many times, always reserved for greater combats, and this recalls the persecutions under Diocletian.
His emblems are the beast of the amphitheater and stones.
The name Agapius comes from the Greek agape, meaning love.

story: Saint Agapius belongs to a hard chapter of the Church's history. In the year 303 the persecution of Christians began across the Roman Empire under the tetrarchy. In Palestine, how harshly the measures were applied changed from year to year and depended on the provincial and imperial authorities. One city became a place of trials, imprisonments and executions: Caesarea Maritima, the seat of the provincial government and an important city of the eastern Mediterranean.

Of Agapius himself, very little is known. The sources say plainly that nothing certain survives about his birth, his family or his work. His memory rests almost entirely on the testimony of Eusebius, who was later bishop of Caesarea and who gathered accounts of the Christians who suffered there. Eusebius lived close to these years and these places, which adds to the value of his account. His writing is not a Roman court record. It is a Christian work of memory, and scholars read it with care.

That account has come down to us in two forms. A short Greek version travels with Eusebius's Church History in part of the manuscript tradition. A longer version survives mainly in Syriac, and William Cureton published and translated it in the nineteenth century. The longer text adds details about the spectacle and speeches attributed to Agapius. These are consistent with the meaning of his witness, but they cannot be treated as a verified transcript. What both versions share is the core: he was exposed to wild beasts in public, he refused to renounce his faith, he survived the first attack, and he was finally put to death by drowning.

According to the Roman Martyrology, Agapius had suffered torments many times before, but each time he was held back for greater combats. Then, during games in the amphitheater at Caesarea, in the presence of Maximinus, he was brought out once more. Eusebius says he was offered his freedom if he would give up the Christian faith. Agapius did not accept. The reason the source gives for his stand is not any common crime. It is faithfulness to the Creator.

A bear was loosed against him in the arena. Eusebius describes Agapius as ready to face the trial, and says the animal wounded him without killing him at once. In the words of the Martyrology, and here it speaks as tradition, he was still breathing. According to the Greek text, he survived a day. Then stones were tied to his feet and he was drowned in the sea. The sea fits Caesarea's coastal setting, though no one can name the exact stretch of shore. Where he was buried, and what became of his body, are not known. The most dramatic details are best read within the language of ancient martyr literature, and the sequence of events rests on Eusebius.

The date is a matter of some care. Eusebius places the event in the fourth year of the persecution and ties Maximinus's arrival to a day in November. Tradition has read this as November 20, 306 for the arena and the following day for the death. The Church's memorial today falls on November 21, though some older calendars kept November 20. The firm fact is that Agapius died at Caesarea during the persecution of the early fourth century. No independent records allow greater precision.

There is also a warning to the careful reader. Eusebius tells of a second Agapius, who was beheaded at Caesarea with seven companions, among them two men named Alexander and two named Dionysius. The Eastern tradition commemorates that group on March 15. The two accounts end in different deaths and must not be merged. The saint remembered on November 21 is the one of the bear and the sea. Some ancient calendars named Agapius together with Timothy and Thecla, and he entered the Latin martyrologies relatively late. The Roman Martyrology today still keeps his praise, recalling his earlier trials, the bear and his death at sea. His emblems in art are the beast of the amphitheater and stones. His name, from the Greek agape, means love. By including him in her calendar, the Church recognizes the holiness of his witness. His holiness lay in a plain fidelity that would not be traded for freedom.

issues: Story paragraph 1: 'four joint rulers' is not in the sources, which say only 'under the tetrarchy'. Removed.
Story paragraph 1: 'One city above all' overstates the source, which says only that Caesarea was a setting for trials, detentions and executions. Softened.
Story paragraph 1: 'a great port' is not in the sources, which call Caesarea an important urban centre of the eastern Mediterranean. Corrected.
Story paragraph 2: 'great weight' overstates the source, which says Eusebius's closeness 'increases the value' of his account but that it still needs critical reading. Reworded.

Spoken beats: no changes needed. The count is 129 words. History and tradition are separated acceptably, the Creator reason is attributed to Eusebius, and nothing is said of Agapius being a bishop (that comes only from Wikipedia, and the Catholic reference says his profession is unknown). The map coordinates for Caesarea Maritima are correct.
factcheck.reviewer_note: The spoken beats label only the drowning as 'tradition', although the Roman Martyrology's 'according to tradition' covers the bear and the drowning together. This is cautious rather than wrong. The Greek text supports 'the next day', and the sources show some date variation (November 20 or 21). Wikipedia's claims that he was a bishop and was held in prison for two years were deliberately left out because the Catholic reference does not support them.

es.name: San Agapio
es.hook: Le ofrecieron la libertad si renunciaba a su fe, pero se negó.
es.summary: San Agapio, mártir de Cesarea en Palestina, rechazó la libertad a cambio de renunciar a su fe, sobrevivió a un oso en el anfiteatro y fue ahogado en el mar en el año 306.
story: San Agapio pertenece a un capítulo difícil de la historia de la Iglesia. En el año 303 comenzó la persecución contra los cristianos en todo el Imperio romano, bajo la tetrarquía. En Palestina, la dureza con que se aplicaron las medidas cambió de un año a otro y dependió de las autoridades provinciales e imperiales. Una ciudad se convirtió en lugar de juicios, encarcelamientos y ejecuciones: Cesarea Marítima, sede del gobierno provincial y ciudad importante del Mediterráneo oriental.

De Agapio mismo se sabe muy poco. Las fuentes dicen con claridad que nada cierto se conserva sobre su nacimiento, su familia o su obra. Su memoria descansa casi por completo en el testimonio de Eusebio, que más tarde fue obispo de Cesarea y que recogió los relatos de los cristianos que sufrieron allí. Eusebio vivió cerca de esos años y de esos lugares, lo cual aumenta el valor de su relato. Su escrito no es un registro de un tribunal romano. Es una obra cristiana de memoria, y los estudiosos la leen con cuidado.

Ese relato ha llegado hasta nosotros en dos formas. Una versión griega breve acompaña la Historia eclesiástica de Eusebio en parte de la tradición manuscrita. Una versión más extensa se conserva sobre todo en siríaco, y William Cureton la publicó y tradujo en el siglo XIX. El texto más largo añade detalles sobre el espectáculo y sobre los discursos atribuidos a Agapio. Son coherentes con el sentido de su testimonio, pero no pueden tratarse como una transcripción verificada. Lo que ambas versiones comparten es el núcleo: fue expuesto a fieras en público, se negó a renunciar a su fe, sobrevivió al primer ataque y finalmente fue dado muerte por ahogamiento.

Según el Martirologio Romano, Agapio había sufrido tormentos muchas veces antes, pero cada vez fue retenido para combates más grandes. Luego, durante los juegos en el anfiteatro de Cesarea, en presencia de Maximino, fue sacado una vez más. Eusebio dice que se le ofreció la libertad si abandonaba la fe cristiana. Agapio no aceptó. La razón que la fuente da para su postura no es ningún crimen común. Es la fidelidad al Creador.

Se soltó contra él un oso en la arena. Eusebio describe a Agapio dispuesto a enfrentar la prueba, y dice que el animal lo hirió sin matarlo de inmediato. En palabras del Martirologio, y aquí habla como tradición, aún respiraba. Según el texto griego, sobrevivió un día. Después le ataron piedras a los pies y lo ahogaron en el mar. El mar encaja con el entorno costero de Cesarea, aunque nadie puede señalar el tramo exacto de la orilla. Dónde fue sepultado y qué sucedió con su cuerpo no se sabe. Los detalles más dramáticos se entienden mejor dentro del lenguaje de la antigua literatura martirial, y la secuencia de los hechos descansa en Eusebio.

La fecha requiere cierto cuidado. Eusebio sitúa el hecho en el cuarto año de la persecución y vincula la llegada de Maximino con un día de noviembre. La tradición lo ha leído como el 20 de noviembre de 306 para el anfiteatro y el día siguiente para la muerte. La memoria actual de la Iglesia cae el 21 de noviembre, aunque algunos calendarios antiguos conservaron el 20 de noviembre. El hecho firme es que Agapio murió en Cesarea durante la persecución de comienzos del siglo IV. No hay registros independientes que permitan mayor precisión.

También hay una advertencia para el lector atento. Eusebio habla de un segundo Agapio, decapitado en Cesarea junto con siete compañeros, entre ellos dos hombres llamados Alejandro y dos llamados Dionisio. La tradición oriental conmemora ese grupo el 15 de marzo. Los dos relatos terminan en muertes distintas y no deben fundirse. El santo recordado el 21 de noviembre es el del oso y el mar. Algunos calendarios antiguos nombraron a Agapio junto con Timoteo y Tecla, y entró en los martirologios latinos relativamente tarde. El Martirologio Romano actual aún conserva su alabanza, recordando sus pruebas anteriores, el oso y su muerte en el mar. Sus atributos en el arte son la fiera del anfiteatro y las piedras. Su nombre, procedente del griego ágape, significa amor. Al incluirlo en su calendario, la Iglesia reconoce la santidad de su testimonio. Su santidad consistió en una fidelidad sencilla que no quiso cambiarse por la libertad.
